projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George Kraincic was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran George J. Kraincic. Mr. Kraincic served in the U. S. Army. He served in the European theater and his highest rank was P4. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Kraincic's home in Willoughby Hills, Ohio, on February 18, 2003. George was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: In 1941 I was living in two places. My sister's house and our 18-acre farm in Willoughby Hills off of Eddy Road.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, when I went to the service I was 20 years old. It was in 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in '41 were you still in high school?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I graduated in February of 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: February of '41?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Working then or --

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: After graduation I was working at the Dresser Muligraff Corporation (ph) in Euclid, Ohio. I spent 36 years there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yes, I do because, also, I served -- I was living in a couple of places. That was because my parents took over the Slovenian Society Hall in Euclid as managers and we were there seven -- six, seven years, so we had a vacant house. I was living at the apartment at the Slovenian Society Hall in Euclid, Ohio, off of Recher Avenue also.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell us as much as you can about hearing about the news of the attack.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I was -- of course, I remember the Pearl Harbor Day. Yeah. I do remember that. I was studying music with Old Timers. I was the youngest singer in the group, I guess. They were a Slovenian group of men that met every Sunday morning. And I happened to go downstairs and for a minute or two and I found out at the bar that Pearl Harbor was attacked.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I guess we all were pretty stunned. Everybody. Bit of calmness already, nothing much, no kind of good time. It was just quiet. Everybody. Didn't know what to say, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You said you were down at the bar. Same reaction from the rest. Were they tempted to go out the next day and sign up?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, some people did. Actually, our area, there was two streets, and there was something like -- they weren't signing up, but they did get drafted, about 25 people on two streets, and it appeared in the newspaper how many people came from a small area. I wasn't in that picture, I don't know why, they missed me. But it was a big group of fellows that finally all got -- most of them got called up by the blood and drafts board. Draft board number 49. They had their offices in Nottingham about -- is that _____+ road in -- near St. Clair.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, did you have job deferments for a while?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yes, I did. It so happened that when I knew that I was going to go in the service I was finally notified that I was going to go to the service, I talked my father into quitting the business, which is a bar business, taking care of the property. I knew he couldn't do it himself. And my sister and my mother, I knew they couldn't handle it, so I asked them to quit and they did quit and went to the farm and actually stayed there on the farm and raised cattle and pigs and chickens and everything. And also they developed a picnic ground which was pretty popular then for people coming out ____+. So he had no income of any kind besides a little bit of that. So actually I was actually called a supporter of the family so I had two deferments. But it wasn't very nice because, you know, I'm working on a hand-screw machine and all around me is women, there's no guys, and it was a very funny situation. All the women squeezing in on me and I said, oh, they are coming from all sides. I am the only guy there left and it was embarrassing. So finally I was able to get another deferment if I wanted I could have had it, but I said no, it's time to go, so I went. It was real embarrassing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that would be about a year-and-a-half after the war started. Do you remember doing everything for the war efforts? Obviously you were working on a war-related industry.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. Funniest thing I was working on the hand-screw machine, and I was working on a brass fuse, a fuse that goes inside of the shell, and it had 80 different operations on it, so it comes out of the 40 millimeter anti-aircraft gun ___+. It was unbelievable. When I went to the service I was in a 40 millimeter outfit. So we had a lot of tricky operations, like I said, it was 80 different operations on a little piece like this, just round, that goes at the end of the shell for a timer, and it should blow up on contact or otherwise. That was 40 millimeters, which 40 millimeters was for low-flying aircraft, not the high flying. The high flying had 90 millimeters. But our unit was a crack outfit, and our lieutenant colonel, he kept volunteering us for funny different missions. It's just unbelievable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were finally drafted in May of '43, right?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I went in in May of '43, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Tell me what you can about your training.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: The training, yeah, we went to -- we didn't know where we were going, we were going west and we wound up in Chicago and then all of a sudden they detoured us down to Georgia, going west and all of a sudden detoured us to the swamps of Georgia near Savannah, about 40 miles from Savannah, Georgia, and that's where we took our basic training. But I made out pretty good on that basic training thing because I was in there about a month, and something happened to the radio operator, the mechanic that we had, he was held over from a cadre, and he left the service. And I got a T4 rating within about a month. It was very shocking. So because of that I don't think I ever did any KP duty. I was able to get away with -- so even in the rougher parts of the training, we spent a lot of time in the swamps, day and night. Night was very scary. Everything was florescent at night in the swamps and the trees were fluorescent and bugs all over. We had to squeeze between narrow trees and it was quite a bit of training. Alligators along the paths, you know. And it was a swamp, you know, I think the Okefenokee swamp. It was a big area and we took a lot of our training, most of our training in the Okefenokee swamp. So consequently we thought we'd be going somewhere in the Pacific or something and, no, and we went over in one of the biggest convoys that ever went over to Europe, 80-ship convoy. Before we got there we served over the winter in Richmond, Virginia, Army air base, so that was more or less just like if we were in Cleveland. There were streetcars were there and main streets and all that stuff and that was good duty. That gave us the start of good duty. Every place we went we had good duty. We didn't have as much suffering as other's had, you know. And we weren't down the front lines having to move all the time. And so that's -- we had a good duty. Plus, we were able to see things nobody else saw because they were too fast on the front line.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about the convoy? Was that a rough crossing?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, it took us -- I think it took us about eight days. There was 80 ships in it. It wasn't tough for me. Again, like I say, our colonel volunteered us for MPs, made up MPs, four or five decks, so we had the run of the ship. Nobody could stop us. But they did assign me to the radio shack. I remember the guy's name, Charlie Doumas (ph) from Chicago, he was a radio ham and I was just a bootlegger on five meters, and I'd send messages. I literally hear messages come on the radio and run them up to the captain's front, you know, for -- do you want me to turn that off?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Did you have any sub scares or anything in the convoy?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sub scares?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, but I guess I'm lucky I'm here. We were traveling -- we went over about 80 days after the invasion. You know, we should have gone over when we were there already. We had one whole battalion out on the island. They thought they were going over. We were backing them up on the beaches. And instead of going over we went up to guard the island. I forgot. I'm drifting here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We were talking about the convoy.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: All right. Oh, yeah, there was constantly, because this was the biggest convoy that went over so they were maneuvering back and forth going different places. But it was -- I was on the John Ericsson and it was a very pretty classy ship. It was a sister ship of the Red Cross ship, Gunshold (ph). Called the Gunshold (ph). Anyway, Swastikas were all over the decks. You know there was brassy and brass, big Swastikas all over the ship, and it was taken over by the United States. Big ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't do anything to remove those Swastikas?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, no, it was a sister ship of the Red Cross ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you arrive in Great Britain?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Seven or eight days later. Let's see, we left on the 13th, I think it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's get your itinerary.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I'm surprised to see some of the things I did. Okay. Well, we moved around. We were at Richmond Army Air Base and then they sent us over to Camp Pickett, Virginia, and just holding us there. We had a few different pieces of training and then we left Camp Pickett, and that's in Virginia, near Richmond, via train. And we arrived in Camp Edwards, Massachusetts. That was -- let's see, May 5th. We arrived at Camp Stewart in May of 1943 is when we started in Camp Stewart. But, anyway, out of Camp Edwards, we embarked there. It is SS John Ericsson, formerly SS Kingsboln. We arrived in Liverpool on May the 23rd. And we disembarked later from Liverpool, England via train to Leek, Staffordshire. Staffordshire. And they were already giving us passes. See, passes to Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent and Newcastle. And if we had spare time we could get passes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do for fun when you had the pass?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Head for any town. I didn't drink, never drank in my life. I used to roam around and see everything. I was a traveler.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Get along okay with the British?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they were very good. You'd go to their door looking for a place to rent or something they'd take you in for nothing, serve you, treat you like a king. Yeah. And then part of our group went to Bushy Park, London. That was where Eisenhower was. And later on, we were -- it doesn't say on here, but we did, we were set up in anti-aircraft guns, different little communities there, but always on the move, you know, in and out, in and out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit at that time?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: 789 anti-aircraft artillery, automatic weapons battalion, semimobile. That means that we didn't have enough vehicles to move and go. We had to go in steps, move up 50 miles and come back and pick up the other guys and move up. You couldn't borrow any trucks because they were all busy on the battlefield.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who were you attached to when you first got there?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I'm trying -- I can't remember who we were attached to at that moment. It don't say on my itinerary either. We were -- one of our outfits, one of our batteries was at Bushy Park, London. June 6th, like I say, we were at -- right on the channel. One battery went out on the island and they thought they were going over to the channel and they didn't go. And then we moved back up north then after, let's see, July 18th, again went up. Let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the --

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I was classified as a radio mechanic but really we operated our radios. I had three transmitters and 12 portable radio receivers. One radio receiver was at every gun section, was just 593, I think it was called, about this big and battery operated and they were wet batteries. I had to maintain the batteries, charging them, and so that's why I was able to get around the gun section there. But while we're still in England I drew up a circuit, amplifying circuit, which you have got in there, too, and I gave it to the rear echelon and some guy, some officers that came down and was questioning me about what is it, what is it, and I explained it to them. He gave me a three-day pass to London because what happened with the circuit was, it was amplifying, just amplifier one, two amplifier section, and the amplifier, and I connected the telephone, the telephone lines, and we also, our communication section was in charge of telephones, too, but I hooked -- I put clips on the ends of the telephone wires and hooked them up to the amplifier system and the telephone and then the guys didn't have to stand there with their phones to their ear. Nobody thought about that, so it was amplified to everybody at the same time. But I never got to go. We moved.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your reward for coming up with that idea was a three-day pass?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, when you were in Great Britain was your main mission to protect against the buzz bombs?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: We did that, and we also -- mostly I think we were in England we were guarding the air fields, fighter fields, fighters, most of them, P51s and P47s. Most of our stay in England was spider -- I mean, fighter. We were at the end of our runways or be halfway up the runway, but we saw a lot of guys get washed out because, especially the P51, and when it comes down it had, you know, had a belly like in there, and would catch the ground and could go almost everywhere because they had a scoop underneath there. And then the P47, when that stuff would come down and crash landing, for some reason they would always catch fire and the bullets always going off so we couldn't get close. Bullets were flying all over. Just boom, boom, boom, boom, all over on the P47, but P47 and P51 were the best planes in the air at that time for the Americans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that became part of your job for crash landing your guys trying to help?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No. They had their own fire department service, no. But they'd come right up to where we were at. We were all buried in the ground all the time. So bullets be flying all over. You had to duck, you couldn't run out the field and try and do anything. The bullets are flying over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memorable attacks or air raids from the Germans while you were there?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, I didn't see any. I heard a lot of warnings, though, but never seen in England. I didn't see because they were headed for London, that's all. And they were shooting buzz bombs, but we were trying to take care of the buzz bombs which were low flying, wasn't high-flying buzz bombs, low-flying buzz bombs. That's what we handled, low flying.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How tough was it to shoot one of those down?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Our outfit was pretty good. That's why I think they just held us, they didn't want us to get killed, I guess, because we were pretty good, set pretty good records for bringing down the buzz bombs, because, you see, they always put them in a pattern, always three ways they come in. There is a booklet here that shows how they come in. Let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ___+ Was there any particular strategy to shooting down the buzz bombs?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, well, yeah, as soon as they started shooting they -- as soon as they started shooting their buzz bombs they had a new pattern all the time and it was always coming in from three directions, stretched out from, like, from Belgium to Holland and Germany. They were coming from different -- mostly from Germany. Yeah, mostly from Germany at that time and Holland. Yeah, two of them come from Germany and one from Holland. And once they start sending them because they had to build these platforms to take them off, see, and we found out right away where the platforms were because with the cameras, the Air Corps found out, so they would last there until we would knock them down so fast they moved overnight or something, they moved to a different location. And we'd always try to locate where they were, but it was hard doing it. Sometimes I went out with the sergeant different places to see where they were coming from exactly, so we could move our guns in the same pattern and they used definite pattern, they had to go straight one way, so we were able to catch up to them. And if you notice there when we were in Antwerp we got about 98 percent of the buzz bombs. We had good guns. We had good operators on guns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So after Great Britain, what was the next stop? Was it France or Belgium? Where did you go from Great Britain?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, we come in on Omaha Beach. Oh, we set up on Omaha Beach to guard the beach for a week or two, I believe it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this soon after D-Day?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, this was in September.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: September of '44?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. It was months after. We left England from Southampton.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were protecting, unloading supplies, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. Well, in England we were, and then when we went over we were protecting the beach, not too long, in Utah, Normandy, at Omaha Beach, and then we also went to Utah Beach. We departed then in Utah Beach and arrived up in Belgium. That was on November 10th. Beersel is where we set up our guns and I set up our radios in Beersel, and then even though the war was there, they was only about 70, 80 miles away, but people were still living the life, you know, just like nothing was wrong.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do for fun then when you had a pass?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Myself I was a dancer. I used to go anyplace I found out there was a dance hall. And I didn't drink so -- I was the only soldier that didn't drink in the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't you get a beer ration like one beer a month or something?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Let's see, if it was beer, I don't remember if it was beer. It was Schnapps we were getting. It was Schnapps. Came in little porcelain bottle like some perfume. No, but I would trade mine for cigarettes or something and then sell the cigarettes. So cigarettes were four or five bucks a pack or something like that. And if you wanted to buy them at the PX anywhere, if you could find a PX, cigarettes were selling for, like, 20 cents a package.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what exactly was the Antwerp X?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: It was a secret command established by General Armstrong. Yeah. It's right in here. It was supposed to be a secret command and nobody know it was going on but they formed such a good organization, they did a good job of organizing and stopping all the flying aircraft that was getting in the buzz bombs, but not the V2 rocket, you couldn't do anything with the V2. I felt the first V2 that came into Antwerp. I was outside of a building and, boy, everything started coming down on the doorway and I jumped back in the building instead of out because a lot of stuff coming down. But the V2s you never knew where they were going to come and you only heard them after they came. It was a thunder roar, like they broke the sound barrier. And I know how true it is, but I understood they could go up 40 miles. I don't know if that's true or not and then come down at an angle and hit the Port of Antwerp. There is no warning. And then later after it blew, later you'd hear that sound barrier, like when you heard a jet break the sound barrier.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was after?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, after it exploded because it went through the air. They had a good bomb there. But our people, they found out where they were at and they kept bombing them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the V2 was silent as opposed to --

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, you couldn't hear it. At night you could see the flame, but it would go at an angle like this and then down like this. And that was in -- they were in Holland and we could see them when we were down in Belgium.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there a lot of V2 attacks while you were there?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Not too many. I don't know why. I think they were trying to do more with London. But see, Antwerp was their -- is where the Germans wanted to get to, so did the Americans. The Americans rushed like mad through the water area, the boats to come in from the boating area and they had no trouble taking over -- I think it was Montgomery wiped out the troops that were heading down around Antwerp from the north. So that's the way it worked there. The Nazis wanted to get to Antwerp because they didn't have the gas and they needed a place to ship to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the Antwerp X mission was to protect Antwerp?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: To protect Antwerp because they knew that the Germans wanted it and so the Americans want it and the Americans won out because of the Bulge. Actually during the Bulge there is story in there, tells in the book that -- how many supplies were coming in through Antwerp for the -- for our troops. But, you know what happened, the Canadians, I mean, Germans were coming so fast, they ran out of supply lines, and they had to stop. That's what they did. And then we got called in on the action of the ground action. Let's see, it was two days after the Bulge started. They told us to drop everything we got because we were living pretty good in Antwerp, so we dumped everything. And it took -- I was in an advance party. I took all my radio men with me, and we were semimobile, so they took us up, I don't know, some 30, 40 miles or so, and then left us there and going to go back and get some more people. And we found a place and took over a dance hall, right close to the street there, cobblestone streets, you know. And at night we had our radios on and we didn't hear nothing. We saw these doll parachutes coming down from the Germans who were dropping baby dolls, about like this, dressed like German soldiers, and they even lit up the sky, the whole sky with phosphorous bombs that you could see them. And we're out there in this little bar, dance hall, bar room right up in town, and I set up all my radios and all of a sudden we hear about one o'clock in the morning we heard this clamp, clunkedly, clunkedly, clunkedly thing. Tanks were going down. We couldn't figure out which tanks they were, so I went around the back building. I crawled up close to the front door on the outside where the bushes were and all that to look to see what these tanks, and I heard they were American tanks, and they were retreating, and we're going the other way. And for two days we are going towards the front, and the tanks are retreating. What they were doing, they were retreating to pinch the Bulge, to cut off the Germans. So we thought we were suicide troops because when they finally -- because the rest of my outfit caught up to me, they set us up, not with my guns, but set up the anti-aircraft guns on the farm roads and we couldn't touch the tank with these little shells. Everything was so confusing. It was unbelievable. You didn't know where you were going with them. So when daybreak broke on the first day we were up on big ridge like, I don't know, a couple hundred feet high, but it was overlooking the valley and here we wake up in the morning and we hear, well, we weren't doing anything at night and all of a sudden when daybreak, shouting like mad, it was right within view of what we were doing, so we beat it out of there. And actually I didn't report in with my outfit, Battery B with my outfit, to the battalion, and the major come looking for me. Balling me out like mad, why didn't I report. I said my captain ordered me not to make any radio transmissions because we were overlooking the field, they were fighting and the ambulances were running all over the place. So I got reprimanded by major, but captain, he is the one that told me not to make the calls yet so. And then we retreated out there. We weren't supposed to be there. But that's the kind of confusion they had all through there. And you should see when the Americans were retreating along that whole front on the northern end, we're going towards the front, and they're leaving the front and they're burning all these gas cans of gas, these five gallons, they had them piled up, must have been 50-foot high and hundreds of feet long, gas cans for our troops. Well, since they were retreating they set all of them on fire and all you saw was these big fires when the Americans were retreating. But what they really were doing, going down the tanks to cut the Bulge off and they had fighting on two sides. That's what broke the back of the Germans. They were fighting them two ways, and pocketed what, 100,000 or something. That's what happened there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The ammo dumps, the fuel dumps --

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, our own gas we had to destroy. Well, we set up finally around November or December, we set up in little towns. I'm trying to remember what their names were. One was LeBrook Chatfontaine (ph). I don't see it in these papers here. But that's what we set up in the mountains. It was real mountainous where we set up. And planes were coming by were French -- I mean German planes. We couldn't depress our guns below 90 degrees straight. The pilots would fly right by you laughing at you and you couldn't hit them with 40 millimeter, flying below where we could hit because we were on mountains and couldn't go down. We could go up, but couldn't go down. They knew it, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they could see you?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. They were laughing at us like, you know, and you could shoot at them with a rifle but that's all we did, if we could. But that was -- it was worse than this. Oh, we had it bad, so bad. I've got some pictures there of how it was. I snuck in a picture of a 40 millimeter. You can't even see it for so much snow. Well, we set up -- after a while we set up to protect them, the City of Liege. That's when it was set up there, so we were south -- no, northeast of the Battle of Bulge then at the time and we were protecting Liege from buzz bombs. And as soon as the troops were overrun, American troops infantry would overrun these launch platforms then when it was clear to the Germans that the sergeant and I, our first sergeant and I, we'd go out and look to see if we could find any kind of evidence there of anything that was new and then we would send it back to rear echelon. And during Christmas, they painted all the buzz bombs red and green for Christmas. They were colored red and green. Would you believe that? We would go out and find them. I have got some pictures here with buzz bomb, the hole it makes, a big hole, makes a big crater like the size of this room.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you could see them, but they were painted red and green?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. And always went to find them wherever they landed, you know. Me and first sergeant would always go and put a couple of guys and we did always find new types of instruments on the motors and all that, you know, different kinds of stuff and turn over to rear echelon because they were getting better and better with the buzz bombs as they went along. I don't have a real good picture of a buzz bomb. I had them stolen. I had them in my book. A lot of friends have them and I asked for them and I haven't gotten them yet, but we are losing everybody in our outfit. We had a lot of reunions across the whole United States and around El Paso and St. Louis, and had them down in Georgia, and had them up Cape Cod, but now all of a sudden nobody wants to run the reunions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about the Bulge?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: It was cold. It was cold but, then again, I was kind of lucky, too, again, because I had these big boxes, probably as big as that chest over there, and had all my radio stuff in there and I could lay that out anywhere and lay on top of it because I was off the ground, but whoever didn't have that would sleep on the ground. It was cold. It was cold. But here, see, there is snow, this is easy, but there was a lot of wind blowing. Oh, it's terrible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything in particular you could do to keep warm, though, other than sleeping off the ground if you could?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, you'd always try to find leaves or something to put them down if you had to sleep on the snow. Anything you could put down you'd try and put it down if you could get it. But, like I said, I was fortunate, I could go in the middle of the woods with that suitcase, I mean case and lay down on it. And we didn't have trucks because we were semimobile so we couldn't sleep on the truck or anything. Cardboard if you could find it was very good if you could find it, but you can't find it in the woods, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So your outfit basically had to wait for trucks from the motor pool to move?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, we only had so many trucks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And half would move and then pick up the other half?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. We had a good outfit. We started together and finished together. We had a real good outfit. That's why they kept volunteering us for some of the hot jobs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And did you have any real close buddies with the outfit?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: They all were. We knew them all. We had reunions and reunions, but now for about three years we hadn't met, but we got some alive yet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: You mean in combat?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: We only lost one guy. That was because he stepped on a land mine. He shouldn't have been there. No, we lost another guy in a truck accident, but that wasn't a combat accident. But that's the one I missed. I was supposed to be on that truck and I wasn't. I missed the truck going back from a little town about 11:30 at night and I missed it, I missed it, so I had to walk six miles to get back and I found out then that one guy got killed. They hit the -- it was a chief, officer, and another one wound up in accident with big two-and-a-half dump truck, so if I had been in that accident I wouldn't have been here. I didn't tell you about that big floating mine that I was this far away from you in a boat. I can't believe that. We were going through and all of a sudden the captain or something in the boat, whoever he was, somehow they saw it, it was floating, it was floating, and he turned the boat so our boat swung down and I'm standing on the rail and boat swung down and I bet you I was anywhere from eight- to ten-foot away from that big mine with the finger sticking up like this, and it was crazy. It just came all of a sudden from nowhere. And then after we passed it up from the channel, took long-range rifle and blew it up. Must have been one that got away somewhere, it was floating in the water. So many times you're in the right place at the right time. I used to go -- every time I could get out of Antwerp because we were bombed 24 hours a day, I would take that 40-mile drive by train to Brussels because Brussels never was touched by bombs except a few bombs that went astray, and I used to go there overnight and used to go dancing in the winter garden, I remember. But one week I didn't come, the room I was staying got bombed by a bomb that shouldn't have been there. You are always somewhere that you could have got killed and you weren't killed. It was terrible. You never knew where to go. Should I stand here or should I stand there? I was standing in a second floor of a building on channel right here on this point here and General Armstrong -- you've got a picture of him here. He was -- I was standing talking to him and first sergeant talking with the General, and all of a sudden we get warning buzz bombs coming straight at us. It was about two stories high, it looked like, and there was a window there, and we see it coming, General and I, and only thing we had there was a big oak table was left of us there, we both went under the table with this General Armstrong. And what happened kind of at the last moment or something, the buzz bomb tipped a little bit and went over the building and hit a break wall on the other side. But so many times, like I say, you're in the right place at the right time, so you are just lucky if you got back, you know. Yeah, this was the guy. He was head of the whole command at that time, but that was a secret mission, Antwerp X. The people didn't know it was there. I guess they didn't want the Germans to find out we had that thing, zero right in. You can see how many came. And that's how many that weren't shot down. These is how many came through there and how many --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That floating mine, was that in the channel?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah, when we were crossing the channel. And so there just lucky again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So anything else about the Bulge?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: It was a crazy place. Nobody knew what they were doing. Nobody. Nobody knew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there some real fear there that the Germans were going to succeed?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, yeah, of course. Especially when they were -- for us, we are going into it and they are retreating and what's going on. But what they did they cut them off about halfway to the Bulge and so then they had two fronts to work on and the Germans couldn't get no supplies from the other end of Antwerp. And I know we lost a lot of men there. The infantrymen, they took the worst beating on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The whole attack then was a total surprise?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: It appears at the time, yeah, when it happened. Because otherwise, yeah, it just happened fast. There was a lot of stories coming out on how it came out. Why is everybody so interested now at this time? It is what, 60 years, almost everybody is still interested in Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Maybe they discussed so much about Pearl Harbor and D-Day that the Bulge is the next thing, every last thing about it. So what came next then after the Bulge?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, after for us, for us, we didn't do much after that except look like we were waiting to go over to Japan. And so we were spending a lot of time in tents set up in somebody's field waiting for orders. But the troops went real fast after the Bulge, and they didn't need us there. So we went back and we set up wherever they need us set up. We did go, at one point went from Belgium, we went down and that's quite a ways from Belgium down to Dijon, Dijon, France, I think by Paris, to an air field down there. And we only went down there for one week and that was to defend the C47s. They were practicing, pulling these gliders, three gliders. We were only there a week or week-and-a-half or so. Was there while they were training, and they got enough training in and then they had the invasion over the Rhine then after we left. And believe it or not later we wound up on the same spot over there ___+

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then you were in Germany then later?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that about?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: That was -- let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that before?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Before we departed Germany, arrived up in Belgium area on June 22nd.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Of '45, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you did not go into Germany until after V-E Day?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, we were -- no, we were in Germany on V Day, up in Wessel, Germany in the brewery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, right. So tell me about that.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: The brewery was loaded with beer and I don't drink. But what happened was we were right alongside of a railroad track and all these displaced persons were coming up, loaded, open box cars, and I mean thousands of them, they were going towards Antwerp, and we gave them a lot of beer. In fact, we even saw a pig running around and we caught that pig and gave it to the people in the box car, and in two minutes they stripped down, killed and stripped down and were hungry. They had nothing to eat ___+

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything in particular to celebrate on that day even though you didn't drink?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. We were shooting down barrage balloons until the officers come across and say you can't do that. They didn't force because they did it, because you had barrage balloons all over us and the guys decided to shoot them down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's something I've never heard. Easy to hit those?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did some souvenir collecting, huh?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah. I had one good thing that happened to me. Wow, this was back in June. June. July. July. July of -- I got a rest leave pass for a week in Chamonleblonc (ph), and we went there for this one week. The whole town was free, bars, movie theaters, everything was free. And I stayed in the Majestic Hotel. I have got pictures of it over there, sixth floor. And I was allowed to bring one guest a day to lunch. The guest was, of course, local people. And there were three girls from Paris. I have a picture. They were there, and so three of us guys, we dated these three girls and brought them to dinner, had symphony music playing and everything for lunch. And you could get anything you wanted there for food, drink, good time. END OF SIDE 1, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Chamonleblonc (ph), have you ever heard of that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: That's where they had the Olympics there six years ago. It was a place where a jet hit one of the cables 10,000 foot up in the air. Well, those are the cables. I have got pictures of them. That was it. And then our weekly stay was to end there and our captain says we have two trucks. See, I told you I was having a good time. He says, well, the war is going to be over soon, he said. And we were standing in the area waiting to be deployed somewhere and he said, let's take the long way home. So we goes in our two trucks, and these are -- you had to back up a truck sometimes to get around a curve in the mountain. And we went through the border guards, first set of border guards, they let us go through. The second one wouldn't let us go into Switzerland, although we were in Switzerland just before that, we took a boat ride out on Lake Geneva, but they wouldn't let us through and captain said, well, we will take the long way home. The war is going to be over soon. We went down south and we went down into Italy and then all the way up through the Brenner Pass, and that was some place way up in the mountains. Desolate land. It was just like a desert up there. So we then we went into Austria, and then we went back to the right again and we went to Munich and went into the Nuremberg Trials. I went to the Nuremberg Trials and stayed there about an hour there in Munich.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you sat in on one of the sessions?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, we went there. Well, they were kind of wide open. It wasn't like I see on TV. We were able to get in, so that was exciting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anybody in particular ___+

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I can't remember, no. In fact, I did talk to -- some of the Russians were great, prevalent there in that building over there. I was able to communicate with them. I'm Slovenian. I was able to communicate somewhat Russian because of the Slovenian language. That was exciting. In the Army, it's not what you did, it's what you got away with. But when we were -- our colonel would volunteer us for the best job. And so, you know, I came back good, healthy, and I could laugh. There were so many of them that didn't come back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were able to send a lot of these souvenirs back then, right?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: After the war was over you were allowed to send, yeah. I'm sorry I didn't send more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So there was no restriction?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Whatever the officers thought we shouldn't have, everything was censored. But the guns, they seem to let us send them, except when we went to go back to the states, they told everybody don't you dare get caught with anything like this we got here. We'll stop the transport and nobody is going to go home, but they didn't check everybody. We had one guy -- oh, we had come back in a bad ship. It looked like a Liberty Ship. We had thousands of people on it and we went through the worst storm they had in the Atlantic. It was in December. Aircraft carrier got their deck warped and that's how bad the storm was and we were all by ourselves out of Marseilles, all the way along the coast and with all those bad waters and the boat could go out of the water and come down. Propeller would go out of the water and come down, but we made it all by ourselves. We come home. We come into the states on Christmas Eve ___+ New Year's Eve. But I did get, when we were in Richmond, Virginia, I was able to get home on Christmas Day just by some -- I didn't have a pass to go to Cleveland, I had a pass to go to Richmond, Virginia. Some spare passes and I made a pass out to Cleveland. And you passed the military police all the time. They check on you. I went to the airport in Washington, D.C., took -- oh, here's what happened. One of my buddies got a truck and drove me to Richmond, Virginia, to the railroad station and pushed me through a window in a train, passenger train, because you couldn't get in the door, it was so full, so many people going to Washington. That was 100 miles away. And pushed me through. I got to the National Airport in Washington and I told them I had to get home, I had to get home. So they took somebody off the plane and put me on. I got a flight to Cleveland, C47. And I got home to Cleveland with the plane. I hitchhiked from Cleveland to Willoughby Hills there where we were living in the woods, and I got just the one day. And my mother was -- somehow I called her, and she said she won't be home, she will be at the Slovenian Hall. So I just got home around midnight to the Slovenian Hall. And that's when I come home. But when I was the first time I came to Cleveland when I got that pass, and then I had to take a train back, I took a 12-hour train from Cleveland to Richmond, Virginia -- no, to Washington. And then I took a taxicab for eight bucks from Washington to Richmond, Virginia. And always had to take five people. It was a $40 a ride. And I gets to -- I get to the Richmond area air base and we're in the woods and when we go out to go to town, we took our boots with us, we had to walk through the mud and everything, and we'd put our boots along a fence, and then hitchhike a ride into Richmond, Virginia. And on our way back we'd look for our boots and go back through the mud and back. Well, I didn't make it for the roll call in the morning. I could hear them calling my name. I was in the woods. I couldn't come out of the woods at that time. And then I'm listening and I'm listening and then there were so many people AWOL, that one day they excused everybody. So I wasn't there for that roll call. It was very exciting in the service for me, only because I came back alive and survived it. Crazy little things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That whole thing was December of '45, I assume?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you when you heard the news that they dropped the first atomic bomb? In Marseilles?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: You know, I can't remember that. That I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still in a staging area?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, but I don't remember. I know I was in Ipswich, England, England, when the President died, Roosevelt died. I remember that. I was in Ipswich, England. I was even able to play golf up there in Ipswich, England. I was just fortunate that I had so much freedom. I wouldn't give it up for all because I came back all right. Even though I took riding lessons on the horses, jumping hurdles, I fell on my knee and hurt it and had to get laid up for a week.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, for the purposes of the tape, let's see, you have a rifle, a Hitler Youth knife, a camera, a couple of flags, a very big flag and smaller flag, and that's a canteen, I assume?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that a German canteen?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, German.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And whatever else. I should have brought a camera.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I've got books. I've got pictures, lot of pictures.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The stuff you brought back from overseas, that is some of the stuff?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I could have if I had known about it sooner.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And let you get away with it?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I don't think too much. Everybody was up in the air, I guess. I can't remember. I know they were at the Slovenian hall for a party when I got there, so there was a party there, even before I got there. But everybody was glad it was over. We lost a lot of people in our area, you know, from the war, but I was just one of the lucky ones.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Probably the -- how good the England and the Belgium people treated us. Of course, we were saving them, but I believe that was -- they were very grateful, very grateful. They even now come to all our, you know, when we have our reunions, especially the National, they always send somebody over from Belgium, always. I don't know what I did with mine. I got an award from Prince of Belgium and one from the Prince of Luxembourg in St. Louis about six, seven years ago ___+. He gave us trinkets to everybody, some kind of memorial, and they brought 26 people over from Belgium to pass out all the stuff they were giving us, little souvenirs. I don't know what I did with mine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the French nice, too?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: The French were not very nice to anybody. You hear that everyday. You hear it now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You still hear it, exactly.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: They still have a lot of, I don't know, something against Americans all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But even back then when you were in France?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I would say so. Well, the Partisians were different than some; but, see, they were in the middle of all this stuff. Everybody was going through their land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No. I guess -- like I said, I was having a good time. I wasn't in the front line so that was fortunate. If I was on the front line I wouldn't be here, I know. Infantry really took a beating. Really took a beating. And some of people were only in Europe a couple of weeks and then had to go to the front line. Young people. But did you look at that book there? A lot of pictures.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There was never a point during the Bulge when you would be asked to become infantry, was there?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Not me. We did give up some people. They needed them. We could see all the firing at night going on toward Bastogne, and we were pretty close. But, well, yeah, I had to put -- sergeant, private, the guard, on Christmas Eve and on New Year's Eve, I remember, because we didn't have enough people. One of the worst things I saw, too, was three B17s when we were in this area, German front there, three B17s that got blown up and come down all at one time. Three of them. You're counting, trying to find out if everybody got out of the ship, you know, parachutes. A lot of them didn't get out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they all go at once? Did one get hit and take the other two or how did that happen?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I don't know how they got hit. There were like three of them flying and all of a sudden they were cracking up, so I don't know. I thought it was from 88 anti-aircraft guns from the Germans, I think. That's what I thought at that time. And we were -- we kept getting strafed from Focke-Wulfs where we were up in the mountains. They would drop flares at us at night and then take pictures, you know, and then come back in the daytime and come back and bomb you. We weren't allowed to shoot at them at night. We had a crazy guy from California, Monkey (ph) his name was, he jumped on a machine gun that was on a truck. There was a Focke-Wulf chasing a P47 and shot in the valley, you could see it shot down the P47 and then the Focke-Wulf came back to do something else again and make another sweep around, but after he shot down the P47 this guy, Monkey guy, it was at night, dark really, and he shot the plane to pieces. 600 rounds a minute anti-aircraft. I mean, the machine guns, four guns going 150 rounds a minute. He brought down a big plane at night in the dark by luck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And your batteries, did you have any close calls with any of those attacks or any raids on your batteries?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Yeah, they always were, but the guys were always dug in sort of. They knew a plane was coming from that direction they'd go against that bank, you know, or the other bank where the planes were coming from. But, yeah, they were trying to get us, but they didn't. It was a time where you never knew every minute what was going to happen, you know. I had one guy in my communication section, he went nuts just from listening to all the stuff on the radio, what's going, coming now and this and that, he went nuts. The trouble was he got married two days before he went overseas. His wife came up to camp and got married then she sent him off with lovey-dovey notes. You can't do that to a guy. "I love you, I need you, I need you." And he came here to my house. I brought him to my house. He had a reunion in Willoughby Heights and I showed him where I lived. I brought him. And he was all right after that. But he's died now since, too. We're all dying. I was 80 on Sunday, last Sunday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Happy birthday. He was listening to ___+

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Mostly he was listening to the plots of where the buzz bombs were coming and where they blew up and all. In fact, it got so bad I had to take him off. I didn't want to tell anybody, but he was going mad and I don't know how the major found out, the doctor found out. He even built a casino in the corner of our quonset hut we had and called it Hatch Casino and he had pictures of his family and everything. And then we didn't want to turn him in, we figured they wouldn't treat him right, but they finally found out and took him away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a lot of letters from home?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, yeah, a lot of girls. Girls, the girls were very good to writing letters and our neighbors all did, always did. You could always expect them -- to get a letter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would they write?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I got some letters somewhere. Just lovey-dovey stuff on what's happening because there was a lot of women left at home, a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No. No. In fact, one of these girls that I sent pictures of me and had them in pictures, about six months ago this one girl she sent -- she sent three or four photographs back to me, she didn't want them anymore, Well, you are getting old now, you are getting rid of stuff now and I couldn't figure that out. It was a trying time. After -- see, we had a good thing going after the war, we started Euclid Veteran's Club, and started in 1945. And about November or December they started. After the I, I mean the first, pardon me, into the club the first of the year, but that club had up to 500 people in it then. We still have over 200, I think, but last year we lost 13 to death who died last year, so we're losing them and now we're thinking about selling our building because the guys are all too old like me and they can't work on that stuff. Just like me, I hurt my arm. I fell in my driveway and I hurt my arm. Can't do what I want to do. You get old, you break everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still a Euclid Slovenic Veteran's Club then?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Still is. We are negotiating with Gazano (ph), Gazano is renting it from us now. He might take it over and we're trying to keep our own room, our private room for the next five or seven years and we're still working on it. And I don't know if he can't get money or what, and we're willing to donate, put up some of the money so he's got money, but the guys can't do nothing. It takes people to run the building, got a big building, two party centers. And we don't want to do it, the guys got enough trouble at home, you know, you don't take care of your own home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers it?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: I guess. Told you, it wasn't much of anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's great. Tell me what you can remember about the USO shows.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Okay. Yeah, we were invited to attend the show. It was out in the open. I believe that it was probably Frankfurt, I'm not sure. But Dale Evans was there and Jimmy Braddock visiting the GIs. Of course, the GIs all had good cameras, and I remember one of the photographers, the GI photographers asked, said, can we have some --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Cheesecake?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: -- cheesecake. And she says to them -- she says, yeah, give me that camera and you can have all the cheesecake you want. That was Dale Evans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was she pretty nice?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Oh, yeah, she was a really nice girl. She married the -- what's his name --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Cowboy Roy Rogers.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Right. And Jimmy Braddock was a boxer. There was a big show that was put on for troops and everybody was invited.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other shows? That was the big one, huh?

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, there was -- after -- we had -- there was what's this guy that played the music? He got lost in a plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Glenn Miller.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Glenn Miller, yeah. I didn't see Glenn Miller, but I saw his band. Trigger Alpert was in charge of it at that time, called Trigger Alpert, and it was -- they didn't come to see us at the field. We were in a hole, dug in a hole, anti-aircraft, but they came to see the Air Force people, but we snuck in. And, yeah -- I'm losing my thought.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right. I just wanted to get a little bit of that. That's okay. It seems like I've asked a lot of guys that question about shows and they didn't remember seeing any shows.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: Well, because they came to the air fields.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's true. You are right. A lot of the guys in infantry not going to come to the front line.

sp.speaker: George Kraincic
sp.p: No, I was a different kind of an outfit. We could go from one end of the country to the other at different times as you can see or just one battery would go out and other one wouldn't go, so we had kind of run of the whole European theater; but I'm just lucky because many a time I should have gotten been -- should have been in bad shape and was at the right place at the right time.
